title: Object storage service
like: a cloud file store like Amazon S3
brief: Customers store billions of files, from tiny pictures to huge videos, and fetch them by name. The service must never lose a file, scale without a limit and stay cheap. Most files are written once and rarely read again.

clarify.q: Can a file change after it is saved?
clarify.a: A new upload replaces it whole. Files are never edited in place.

clarify.q: How safe must a file be?
clarify.a: Never lost. Once saved, a file must be there years later, even if a data centre burns down.
No. A small share is read all the time and most are almost never touched.

notes: Uploads average a few MB. Use the request mix to work out their peak rate.
Around 2 PB stored, growing every day (approx.).

numbers.label: Stored data
numbers.how: About 2 PB. Cold storage is roughly a fifth of the price of hot storage (approx.).

hints: Two different jobs hide here: finding a file by name, and storing its bytes. Should one database do both?
Keep a small metadata store that maps a name to where the bytes live, and keep the bytes in object storage. Move cold files to cheaper tiers.

Concurrent commits need protection from garbage collection; durability includes metadata and repair across failure domains. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Separate the name from the bytes. A scalable metadata store answers "where is this file", object storage holds the bytes in several copies, a CDN serves the popular few, and a background job pushes cold files to cheap storage.

designs.name: Metadata store, object storage, CDN and tiering
designs.why: Names go through a store built for huge key lookups. Bytes sit in object storage with copies in several zones. The CDN takes hot reads off it and a lifecycle job moves old files to the archive.

tradeoffs: Keeping several copies protects against loss but multiplies the storage bill. Erasure coding gives similar safety for less.
Cold tiers are cheap to keep and slow or costly to read. Move a file there only when it is truly idle.
A CDN speeds up popular files but may serve a stale version for a short time after a replace.
Strong "read your own write" is simpler for customers but limits how far the metadata store can be spread.
editorial.realWorld: The biggest object stores hold trillions of files and answer tens of millions of requests a second. Durability is promised at eleven nines, and old data costs a fraction of a cent per GB-month (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Object storage service: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Publish only complete durable objects and reclaim unreferenced pieces safely. Readers must never see a partially committed object. An upload id and conditional manifest publication make retries repeatable. Concurrent commits need protection from garbage collection; durability includes metadata and repair across failure domains.

fields.label: Step 1. Upload U has three of four pieces. May its object name become readable?
options: Keep it uncommitted until every piece and checksum is durable
Publish the name now and fill the missing piece later
fields.explanation: Readers must never see a partially committed object.

fields.label: Step 2. The final commit reply is lost. Client retries U. What happens?
options: Create another visible version for every retry
Conditionally commit U once and return the existing object version
fields.explanation: An upload id and conditional manifest publication make retries repeatable.

fields.label: Step 3. A cleanup worker finds old pieces while U is committing. Delete them?
options: Delete only after proving no live manifest or upload references them, with a grace period
Delete anything older than the upload timeout immediately
fields.explanation: Concurrent commits need protection from garbage collection; durability includes metadata and repair across failure domains.

correctness.responsibility: Publish only complete durable objects and reclaim unreferenced pieces safely.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
